Generality lens: (1) The move is stated beyond the example — applicability.use_when/avoid_when and the README 'When to use it, and when not' name the general condition (a goal reduced by a few normalising lemmas to one decidable hypothesis Q whose two sides are each a named project theorem, with self-contained disjoint children), not FLT-specifics. (2) 'When not to use' is honest and specific: three concrete failure conditions (per-side differing normalisation; Q not decidable without classical assumptions; one side a family of subgoals), and consequences name the exhaustiveness obligation, the per-branch hypothesis mismatch, and a concrete failure mode (a reduction dropping a hypothesis a child needs). (3) It says what makes the leaves good for a bounded prover: 'Each child is a good leaf because its statement is self-contained (every hypothesis explicit in the header) and its proof closes from named siblings, not the parent's local context.' The copied code confirms all three: parent is 7 proof lines with one by_cases and one exact per branch (FltRegular.lean:26-28), and both children carry fully explicit hypotheses in their headers.
